messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos, a 54‑year‑old owner of a family‑run hardware store in a modest suburb of Houston, arrived at the clinic on a bright Tuesday with the heavy weight of the past pressing against his chest. He had been a relief worker in the war‑torn region of northern Iraq when a routine supply convoy was ambushed. The convoy’s front row was riddled by a volley of gunshots that tore through the dust and glass of a ruined warehouse. Carlos was pressed forward by the rush of artillery, a shrapnel splinter lodged in his left forearm, and the deafening roar that seemed to swallow the world. In that instant he felt the air itself shift, the walls of the warehouse collapsing around him, and the world recede into a cacophony of screams and explosions. He was never far from the front; proximity to the frontline had become a lived reality, and the memory of those gunshots remains etched in the back of his mind, a phantom echo that now reverberates whenever he hears a distant blast of any kind. From the moment of that assault, certain sounds, sights, and even feelings have become automatic triggers. The sound of a gunshot, even in a supermarket aisle or a neighbor’s kitchen, sends a jolt through his body, forcing him into the same claustrophobic panic he felt among the ruins. The very idea of happiness—his wife’s laughter or the simple joy of closing a sale on a warm day—creates a confusing paradox. Positive emotions, for him, feel precarious; the brighter a moment, the sharper the fear that a gunshot might erupt and crush it. And when he is in close physical proximity to another person—handing out tools or negotiating prices—the sense of being surrounded triggers a sense of impending danger, as if someone could just as easily step into his life and pull a trigger. Each of these triggers sets off a chain of maladaptive strategies. The first is rumination. When the gunshot sounds in the distance flare his memories, Carlos sits in the back corner of his shop and spirals over why the attack had happened to him. He thinks of the convoy’s routes, the orders he had received, the people he had lost. The questions loop relentlessly, and the answers never seem to settle. Second, he has taken to carrying a handgun to the store. He says the feeling of having something sharp at his side keeps him prepared, as if a sudden blast could come from a passing customer or a street vendor. Finally, Carlos finds himself embroiled in petty arguments over seemingly minor disputes—whether a customer feels the wrong price or a contractor misplaces a bolt. The fights, he rationalizes, are a distraction, a way to keep his mind away from the impossible silence of his past. The relationship between these triggers and strategies is cyclical. The first connection—triggers leading to maladaptive strategies—plays out every time a distant crack of gunfire hits his radio. The flash of the memory forces him to ruminate, to replay the convoy in his mind, to cling to the handgun he keeps in his pocket, and to test the boundaries of his tolerance by pushing a neighbor to the brink of confrontation. Each action reinforces the next: rumination amplifies his belief that the past is inescapable; carrying a weapon heightens his hypervigilance, making ordinary noises feel more dangerous; and seeking conflict forces him into closer proximity to others, which itself is a trigger. The second connection—maladaptive strategies feeding back into triggers—becomes evident when Carlos’s presence of the handgun in the store triggers nervous customers, and their unease creates new situations of proximity. In a recent dispute with a long‑time supplier, the argument escalated so far that the supplier’s car had to be moved, the space between them narrowed, and the close physical distance sparked an old, vivid fear of being trapped in a blast. These intertwined patterns have begun to erode the fabric of his daily life. The business, once a source of pride and stability, now feels like a minefield. Sales dip during the hours he is most on edge; his wife, Ana, worries that he is becoming paranoid and pushes him to stay home from the shop more often. The arguments that used to be brief flare into tense standoffs that linger long after the store closes. Carlos now sees his own routine as a battle he cannot win, and the more he tries to fight it, the deeper he sinks into the memories he cannot shake. He came to therapy because one night he found himself standing in the doorway of his shop, staring at the faint silhouette of his own reflection in the glass. The gunshot noise of a distant traffic accident pierced the air, and the old panic rose so swiftly that he felt his throat tighten. He realized that the only thing left that might change the outcome was help. He is most afraid that the cycle will never break, that his life will stay haunted by the echoes of war. Yet he also holds a fragile hope that, through understanding and a new set of coping tools, he might finally let the gunshots in his mind fall silent and reclaim the peace he once found behind the counter of his hardware store.
